warmup.q: A shop's details are kept in Redis for an hour (EX 3600) and read 100 times a second by one copy of the app. Loading them from the database takes 200 ms. Then the hour ends and the key expires. The app follows a simple rule: ask Redis first, and if the key isn't there, load the details from the database and put them back in Redis. About how many database queries does that one copy send for this one shop?
options: 1: the first request reloads it and the rest find it in Redis
About 20: one for each request that arrives during the 200 ms load
100 or more if the requests arrive together: every one that finds nothing before the reload finishes asks the database
0: Redis reloads expired keys from the database by itself
warmup.why: Nothing tells the other requests that a load is already under way, so every request that finds the key missing before the first SET lands asks the database too. When the requests arrive together, that's all of them: in the lesson's demo, 100 requests that missed at once made 100 database calls. At a steady 100 a second, it would be about 20, one per request during the 200 ms. Redis never loads anything by itself; with this rule, your code does.

sections.h: Ask Redis first, load from the database on a miss: cache-aside
sections.html:
Every card payment goes through a fraud check, a piece of code that looks for signs of a stolen card. It needs the shop's details: its name, its country and its category code, a four-digit number that says what kind of shop it is (5940 is a bicycle shop). The details live in the merchants table of the app's database, the system of record that holds the official copy of every fact. Reading one row, the record for one shop, costs about 120 ms, counting the round trip, the time a request takes to reach the database and the answer to come back. At 2,000 payments a second, that's 2,000 queries a second for rows that change maybe once a month.

A cache keeps a copy of often-read rows somewhere faster. The simplest version is a map, a structure that stores a value under each key, inside the app itself. It breaks once the app runs as several copies. Busy apps run, say, 20 copies of the same program on several machines, so that one can fail and the work is shared. Each copy loads every shop for itself, so the database still sees 20 loads per shop. And when a shop changes, there are 20 old copies to fix and no way to reach them. A shared Redis fixes both. There's one copy of each row, and every copy of the app reaches it in well under a millisecond.

Back at the bakery, the shelf is the cache, the baker is the database, and each loaf is one copy of a row. The usual way to run the shelf is cache-aside, also called lazy loading, and the app does all the work:

  1. GET merchant:m-17. If Redis has the key, that's a hit: decode the row and return it.
  2. If it doesn't, that's a miss: load the row from the database.
  3. SET merchant:m-17 <row> EX 3600, so the next reader finds it, and return.

Redis never talks to the database. It holds whatever your code put there, for as long as the key's TTL, its time to live, allows (Expiry, eviction and memory showed how keys expire).

Why caches work: latency, locality and hit ratios gave us the arithmetic for what this buys. Say a hit takes 0.3 ms and a miss 120 ms. With a 95% hit ratio, the share of reads that are hits, the average read takes 0.95 × 0.3 + 0.05 × 120 = 6.3 ms. At 99%, it takes 1.5 ms. Near the top, every point of hit ratio is worth a lot, so everything that causes misses matters: a cache that starts empty, evictions, and TTLs that are too short.

The TTL is also your budget for stale data, copies that are out of date. A shop renamed in the database keeps its old name in the cache until the key expires or your code deletes it. An hour is fine for a shop's name on a screen. It isn't fine for a card's blocked flag. Like the sell-by date on a loaf, the TTL says how long an old copy may sit on the shelf.

A TTL is how long a wrong answer may live. Choose it for each kind of data.

Cache-aside puts all the work in your code. Next, we'll meet four patterns that move part of it elsewhere, and the one rule for writes.

try.title: Time a miss and three hits
steps: From the labs folder, start Redis if it isn't running: docker compose -f env/redis.yml up -d. Docker is a program that runs other programs in sealed boxes called containers, and this command starts Redis in one.

Run CacheAsideDemo (Java) or CacheAsideDemoKt (Kotlin) with the command shown. Gradle, the tool that builds and runs the labs' code, compiles it first. The demo's "database" is a function that sleeps 120 ms per query. Predict the four timings before you run it.
Run it a second time without deleting anything first. What changes, and why? (The demo deletes the key at the start, so look closely.)

code.title: CacheAsideDemo.java
code.html: package sfz.cache.l06.demo; import redis.clients.jedis.RedisClient; import redis.clients.jedis.params.SetParams; /** Cache-aside in front of a "database" that takes 120 ms: one miss, then hits. */ public class CacheAsideDemo { static int dbCalls = 0; // the system of record: in production an Oracle query behind a connection pool static String loadFromDatabase(String id) throws InterruptedException { dbCalls++; Thread.sleep(120); return id + "|Fietsen Utrecht|NL|5940"; } static String getMerchant(RedisClient redis, String id) throws InterruptedException { String key = "merchant:" + id; String cached = redis.get(key); // 1. ask Redis first if (cached != null) return cached; String row = loadFromDatabase(id); // 2. a miss: go to the database redis.set(key, row, SetParams.setParams().ex(3_600)); // 3. keep it for an hour return row; } public static void main(String[] args) throws InterruptedException { try (RedisClient redis = RedisClient.builder().hostAndPort("localhost", 6379).build()) { redis.del("merchant:m-17"); redis.get("warm-up"); // open a pooled connection first for (int i = 1; i <= 4; i++) { long t0 = System.nanoTime(); String row = getMerchant(redis, "m-17"); System.out.printf("read %d: %-30s %7.2f ms (database calls so far: %d)%n", i, row, (System.nanoTime() - t0) / 1e6, dbCalls); } System.out.println("TTL merchant:m-17 = " + redis.ttl("merchant:m-17") + " s"); } } }

alt.title: CacheAsideDemo.kt
alt.html: package sfz.cache.l06.demo import redis.clients.jedis.RedisClient import redis.clients.jedis.params.SetParams /** Cache-aside in front of a "database" that takes 120 ms: one miss, then hits. */ private var dbCalls = 0 // the system of record: in production an Oracle query behind a connection pool private fun loadFromDatabase(id: String): String { dbCalls++ Thread.sleep(120) return "$id|Fietsen Utrecht|NL|5940" } private fun RedisClient.getMerchant(id: String): String { val key = "merchant:$id" get(key)?.let { return it } // 1. ask Redis first val row = loadFromDatabase(id) // 2. a miss: go to the database set(key, row, SetParams.setParams().ex(3_600)) // 3. keep it for an hour return row } fun main() { RedisClient.builder().hostAndPort("localhost", 6379).build().use { redis -> redis.del("merchant:m-17") redis.get("warm-up") // open a pooled connection first for (i in 1..4) { val t0 = System.nanoTime() val row = redis.getMerchant("m-17") println("read %d: %-30s %7.2f ms (database calls so far: %d)".format(i, row, (System.nanoTime() - t0) / 1e6, dbCalls)) } println("TTL merchant:m-17 = ${redis.ttl("merchant:m-17")} s") } }

try.expect: The first read is a miss at about 125 ms (read 1: m-17|Fietsen Utrecht|NL|5940 127.73 ms (database calls so far: 1)). Reads 2 to 4 are hits, from well under a millisecond to about 2 ms. The first hit is often the slowest, because the JVM, the program that runs Java and Kotlin code, speeds code up only after it has run a few times. The database count stays at 1, and TTL merchant:m-17 = 3600 s. A second run looks the same, because the demo deletes the key first: every fresh start of the program begins with one miss. Your numbers depend on your computer and on Docker.

sections.h: Five ways to run a cache: who loads, who writes, and when
sections.html:
Cache-aside is one of five common patterns, and two questions tell them apart. On a miss, who loads the row? On a write, who writes the database and the cache, and when? Cache-aside answers "your code" to all of it. The other four hand part of the work to a cache library, a ready-made piece of code your program uses.

Pattern Who loads on a miss Who writes, and when
Cache-aside your code your code: the database, then DEL the key
Read-through the cache, through a loader you register pair it with one of the write patterns
Write-through the cache: the database first, before put returns
Write-behind the cache: itself now, the database later, in batches
Refresh-ahead the cache, before the entry expires

Read-through moves the miss into the cache. Your code calls get(id), and on a miss the cache calls a loader, a function you gave it. Caffeine, a popular cache library for Java, does this with its LoadingCache, inside one running program. Coherence, a cache product from the database company Oracle, calls the loader a CacheStore. Write-through moves writes there too: put returns only after the database has stored the value, so every write takes as long as the database. That alone doesn't keep the two in step. Coherence's docs say it can't make the two writes succeed or fail together, so one can succeed while the other fails.

Write-behind answers put at once and writes the database later. Coherence waits a set delay after a key's first change, so ten changes to one key within that delay become one database write. Its docs also name the price. Until its queue of waiting writes drains, the cache holds the only copy of the newest data. And changes may reach the database in a different order from the one they happened in. If the machine holding the cache dies with writes queued, they're gone. Keep it away from anything that moves money.

Refresh-ahead reloads entries before they expire. With a 60-second expiry and Coherence's refresh-ahead factor of 0.5, a read in the first 30 seconds returns the cached value. A read between 30 and 60 seconds returns it and starts a reload in the background. Only a read after 60 seconds waits. Caffeine's refreshAfterWrite works the same way. The last section shows a version with no fixed window.

For payments, use cache-aside and keep the database the one source of truth. Its write path has one rule: commit, then DEL the key. (A commit is the moment the database makes a change permanent.) Don't SET the new row instead. Two writers' SETs can reach Redis in the opposite order from their commits, while two deletes in any order leave the same empty key. And don't delete before the commit, or a reader that misses in between puts the old row back.

Commit, then delete the cached copy. Never write the new row into it.

One race survives even the right order. The simulator below lets you play it, and the next lesson takes it apart. Until then, the TTL caps how long a wrong copy can last, which is why every entry gets one. That handles writes. Next, two ways that reads alone can hurt.

sim.title: A reader puts an old row back
sim.intro: cache = 0 means no key; the numbers are row versions. The writer commits version 2 and deletes the key. Can you end with the cache holding version 1?

goal.say: Stale: the database has version 2, and the cache will serve version 1 until its TTL ends. The reader read before the commit and wrote after the delete. Lesson 7 is about this race.

sections.h: Keys that expire together, and lookups for shops that don't exist
sections.html:
Two patterns of reads hurt cache-aside, even when the code is right.

The first is keys that expire together. Say the app restarts and fills the cache with 50,000 shops in one minute, all with EX 3600. An hour later, they all expire within the same minute, and every read in that minute misses. That's 50,000 extra queries for the database on top of its normal load. Meanwhile, the cleanup round from Expiry, eviction and memory deletes 50,000 keys on Redis's single thread, the one that also runs every command. Then the app reloads them all in the same minute again, and the spike comes back every hour.

The fix is jitter: a random spread on each TTL. With 3600 × (1 ± 0.1), the same 50,000 keys expire across 12 minutes instead of one, about 4,200 a minute instead of 50,000. Each reload draws a new random TTL, so the spread holds from then on. It costs one line of code. Some entries live 6 minutes longer than the hour, which is fine for data you already accepted as an hour stale. At the bakery, it's staggering the sell-by dates, so the shelf never empties all at once.

The second pattern is lookups for things that don't exist. Another company's program keeps sending payments for shop ids that were never created. Or a scraper, a program that tries id after id, walks through them. Each lookup misses in Redis, finds nothing in the database, and caches nothing, because there was nothing to cache. So every one goes to the database, every time. This is called cache penetration.

The fix is negative caching: cache the "not found" as well. Store a marker that can't be a real row, such as <missing>, with a short TTL: 60 seconds instead of an hour. Keep it short, because a shop created a minute later should show up without waiting an hour. Your read path now has three cases to tell apart. nil from Redis means "not cached, go and look". The marker means "known to be missing, return nothing". Anything else is a row.

The lab's MerchantCache does both: rows get a TTL with jitter, and missing ids get a 60-second marker.

Jitter spreads many keys apart. It can't help one key that everyone wants at the same moment.

try.title: See jitter spread the deadlines
steps: Open redis-cli, Redis's own window for typing commands: docker compose -f env/redis.yml exec redis redis-cli. Paste the first two commands. Each EVAL runs a small program, written in the Lua language, inside Redis as one command. These two write 10,000 keys with exactly 3,600 seconds, and 10,000 more with 3,600 seconds plus or minus 10%.
The next two EVALs count, for each family of keys, how many expire in each minute from now. Predict both answers first.
Run the last four commands: a negative entry for a shop that doesn't exist. Which GET tells you "known missing", and which "never looked"?

code.title: at the redis-cli prompt
code.html:
EVAL "for i = 1, 10000 do redis.call('SET', 'flat:' .. i, 'x', 'EX', 3600) end return 1" 0
EVAL "for i = 1, 10000 do redis.call('SET', 'jit:' .. i, 'x', 'EX', math.floor(3600 * (0.9 + 0.2 * math.random()))) end return 1" 0
EVAL "local h = {} for i = 1, 10000 do local m = math.floor(redis.call('TTL', KEYS[1] .. i) / 60) h[m] = (h[m] or 0) + 1 end local out = {} for m in pairs(h) do table.insert(out, m) end table.sort(out) for i, m in ipairs(out) do out[i] = 'minute ' .. m .. ': ' .. h[m] end return out" 1 flat:
EVAL "local h = {} for i = 1, 10000 do local m = math.floor(redis.call('TTL', KEYS[1] .. i) / 60) h[m] = (h[m] or 0) + 1 end local out = {} for m in pairs(h) do table.insert(out, m) end table.sort(out) for i, m in ipairs(out) do out[i] = 'minute ' .. m .. ': ' .. h[m] end return out" 1 jit:
SET merchant:m-404 "<missing>" EX 60
GET merchant:m-404

try.expect: The flat family answers with a single line, 1) "minute 60: 10000" (or minute 59 if a second ticked over): every key dies in the same minute. The family with jitter spreads over 12 lines, from minute 54 to minute 65, with roughly 800 to 880 keys each. Then SET prints OK, GET merchant:m-404 returns "<missing>" (known missing: return nothing and skip the database), TTL is (integer) 60, and GET merchant:m-405 returns (nil) (nothing cached: go to the database). math.random gives different numbers on every run, so your counts for the jitter family will differ a little from these.

sections.h: A hundred requests miss the same key at once: the stampede
sections.html:
Now take the busiest shop on a sale day, merchant:m-17, read 100 times a second by each copy of the app. When its TTL ends, the next requests all miss before any of them has put the row back, because loading takes 200 ms. Every one of them goes to the database for the same row. In the lesson's demo, 100 requests that missed at once made 100 database calls. The database runs one query 100 times. The app shares a connection pool, a fixed set of 20 open connections to the database. The pool queues the other 80 queries, and every other query in the app waits behind them. This is a cache stampede, also called a thundering herd: the hundred customers walking to the back of the bakery.

Inside one running program, the fix is single-flight: let the first miss load, and make the others wait for its result. At the bakery, it's the first customer telling the others, "I've asked, wait here." In Java, a ConcurrentHashMap<String, CompletableFuture<Merchant>> is enough. A ConcurrentHashMap is a map that many threads, paths of work running at the same time, can use safely. A CompletableFuture is a box that will hold a result later, and other threads can wait on it.

Each thread that misses makes its own empty future and tries to put it into the map under the shop's key with putIfAbsent, which adds it only if the key has no entry yet. The first thread to succeed becomes the leader and queries the database. The others find the leader's future already there and join() it, which means they wait. When the load ends, the leader puts the row in the future, and every waiter wakes up with the same value. Then the leader removes the entry, so the next miss starts a fresh load. Caffeine's Cache.get(key, loader) does the same for you. In the demo, single-flight took 100 database calls down to 1, and everyone waited about 210 ms, one query's time.

Single-flight only reaches threads inside the same running program. The demo calls each copy of the app a pod, a name borrowed from tools that run many copies of a program. With 4 pods, single-flight made 4 calls, so 20 copies would make 20. Here the bakery picture breaks: in a shop, everyone can see the queue at the baker, but copies of an app see nothing of each other. They need a sign on a shared board.

Redis is that board. The copy that wins SET lock:merchant:m-17 <token> NX PX 2000 loads the row. NX means only if the key doesn't exist yet, PX 2000 deletes the key after 2,000 ms, and the token is a random value that says whose lock it is. The others check the cache every 10 ms for up to a second, then give up and load the row themselves. The demo made 1 call across 4 pods. This lock only saves work: if it fails, two copies load the same row, which does no harm. Locks that must never fail are another matter, and the Faults, time and truth track's lesson Leases, locks and fencing tokens takes them on.

The last option avoids the miss altogether: refresh a busy key before it expires, without a timer and without a stampede of refreshes.

frames.say: This is a cache stampede. The database runs the same query 100 times. With a pool of 20 connections, 80 requests queue for a connection, so they wait far longer than 200 ms, and every unrelated query in the app waits behind them too. In the lesson's demo, 100 requests that missed at once made 100 database calls.

frames.say: After 200 ms, the leader writes the row back with a TTL that has jitter, and puts the row in its future. All 99 followers wake up with the same value, and the leader removes the map entry, so a later miss starts a fresh load. frames.say: Single-flight works inside one running program, one JVM (the program that runs Java and Kotlin code). Twenty copies each have their own map, so the database still gets 20 queries. To get to one, the copies coordinate through Redis: the one that wins SET lock:merchant:m-17 <token> NX PX 2000 loads the row, and the others check the cache for a moment. In the demo, 4 pods made 4 calls with single-flight and 1 with the lock.

try.title: Count the database calls in a stampede
steps: Run StampedeDemo (Java) or StampedeDemoKt (Kotlin). It sends 100 requests at once for a key that isn't in Redis, four times: with no protection, with single-flight in 1 pod, with single-flight in 4 pods (25 requests each), and with a Redis lock across the 4 pods. Each pod is one pretend copy of the app, with its own connection to Redis.
Predict the database calls for each line, and whether the lock makes anyone wait longer.
Read redisLock(). What happens to the waiting pods if the lock holder crashes before its SET?

code.title: StampedeDemo.java
code.html: package sfz.cache.l06.demo; import redis.clients.jedis.RedisClient; import redis.clients.jedis.params.SetParams; import redis.clients.jedis.util.CompareCondition; import java.util.ArrayList; import java.util.List; import java.util.UUID; import java.util.concurrent.CompletableFuture; import java.util.concurrent.ConcurrentHashMap; import java.util.concurrent.CountDownLatch; import java.util.concurrent.ExecutorService; import java.util.concurrent.Executors; import java.util.concurrent.atomic.AtomicInteger; /** 100 requests miss the same cold key at once. How many reach the 200 ms database? */ public class StampedeDemo { static final String KEY = "merchant:m-17"; static final AtomicInteger dbCalls = new AtomicInteger(); static String loadFromDatabase() { dbCalls.incrementAndGet(); sleep(200); return "m-17|Fietsen Utrecht|NL|5940"; } /** One service instance: its own Redis client and its own in-process single-flight map. */ static final class Pod { final RedisClient redis = RedisClient.builder().hostAndPort("localhost", 6379).build(); final ConcurrentHashMap<String, CompletableFuture<String>> flights = new ConcurrentHashMap<>(); String plain() { // cache-aside, no protection String v = redis.get(KEY); if (v != null) return v; v = loadFromDatabase(); redis.set(KEY, v, SetParams.setParams().ex(3_600)); return v; } String singleFlight() { // one load per key per pod String v = redis.get(KEY); if (v != null) return v; CompletableFuture<String> mine = new CompletableFuture<>(); CompletableFuture<String> running = flights.putIfAbsent(KEY, mine); if (running != null) return running.join(); // a follower waits for the leader try { String row = redis.get(KEY); // filled while we became leader? if (row == null) { row = loadFromDatabase(); redis.set(KEY, row, SetParams.setParams().ex(3_600)); } mine.complete(row); return row; } finally { flights.remove(KEY, mine); } } String redisLock() { // one load per key across all pods String v = redis.get(KEY); if (v != null) return v; String token = UUID.randomUUID().toString(); if (redis.set("lock:" + KEY, token, SetParams.setParams().nx().px(2_000)) != null) { try { v = loadFromDatabase(); redis.set(KEY, v, SetParams.setParams().ex(3_600)); return v; } finally { // Redis 8.4+: delete the lock only if it is still ours (it may have expired and gone to another pod) redis.delex("lock:" + KEY, CompareCondition.valueEq(token)); } } for (int i = 0; i < 100; i++) { // someone else is loading: wait for the cache sleep(10); v = redis.get(KEY); if (v != null) return v; } return loadFromDatabase(); // waited a second: load it ourselves } } interface Strategy { String get(Pod pod); } static void run(String label, int pods, Strategy strategy) throws Exception { List<Pod> fleet = new ArrayList<>(); for (int i = 0; i < pods; i++) fleet.add(new Pod()); fleet.get(0).redis.del(KEY, "lock:" + KEY); dbCalls.set(0); ExecutorService threads = Executors.newFixedThreadPool(100); CountDownLatch start = new CountDownLatch(1); List<CompletableFuture<String>> requests = new ArrayList<>(); for (int i = 0; i < 100; i++) { Pod pod = fleet.get(i % pods); requests.add(CompletableFuture.supplyAsync(() -> { await(start); return strategy.get(pod); }, threads)); } long t0 = System.nanoTime(); start.countDown(); requests.forEach(CompletableFuture::join); System.out.printf("%-40s database calls: %3d %4d ms%n", label, dbCalls.get(), (System.nanoTime() - t0) / 1_000_000); threads.shutdown(); fleet.forEach(p -> p.redis.close()); } public static void main(String[] args) throws Exception { run("no protection, 1 pod", 1, Pod::plain); run("single-flight, 1 pod", 1, Pod::singleFlight); run("single-flight, 4 pods", 4, Pod::singleFlight); run("Redis lock (SET NX PX), 4 pods", 4, Pod::redisLock); } static void sleep(long ms) { try { Thread.sleep(ms); } catch (InterruptedException e) { throw new RuntimeException(e); } } static void await(CountDownLatch latch) { try { latch.await(); } catch (InterruptedException e) { throw new RuntimeException(e); } } }

alt.title: StampedeDemo.kt
alt.html: package sfz.cache.l06.demo import redis.clients.jedis.RedisClient import redis.clients.jedis.params.SetParams import redis.clients.jedis.util.CompareCondition import java.util.UUID import java.util.concurrent.CompletableFuture import java.util.concurrent.ConcurrentHashMap import java.util.concurrent.CountDownLatch import java.util.concurrent.Executors import java.util.concurrent.atomic.AtomicInteger /** 100 requests miss the same cold key at once. How many reach the 200 ms database? */ private const val KEY = "merchant:m-17" private val dbCalls = AtomicInteger() private fun loadFromDatabase(): String { dbCalls.incrementAndGet() Thread.sleep(200) return "m-17|Fietsen Utrecht|NL|5940" } /** One service instance: its own Redis client and its own in-process single-flight map. */ private class Pod { val redis: RedisClient = RedisClient.builder().hostAndPort("localhost", 6379).build() private val flights = ConcurrentHashMap<String, CompletableFuture<String>>() fun plain(): String { // cache-aside, no protection redis.get(KEY)?.let { return it } val v = loadFromDatabase() redis.set(KEY, v, SetParams.setParams().ex(3_600)) return v } fun singleFlight(): String { // one load per key per pod redis.get(KEY)?.let { return it } val mine = CompletableFuture<String>() flights.putIfAbsent(KEY, mine)?.let { return it.join() } // a follower waits for the leader try { val row = redis.get(KEY) ?: loadFromDatabase().also { // filled while we became leader? redis.set(KEY, it, SetParams.setParams().ex(3_600)) } mine.complete(row) return row } finally { flights.remove(KEY, mine) } } fun redisLock(): String { // one load per key across all pods redis.get(KEY)?.let { return it } val token = UUID.randomUUID().toString() if (redis.set("lock:$KEY", token, SetParams.setParams().nx().px(2_000)) != null) { try { return loadFromDatabase().also { redis.set(KEY, it, SetParams.setParams().ex(3_600)) } } finally { // Redis 8.4+: delete the lock only if it is still ours (it may have expired and gone to another pod) redis.delex("lock:$KEY", CompareCondition.valueEq(token)) } } repeat(100) { // someone else is loading: wait for the cache Thread.sleep(10) redis.get(KEY)?.let { return it } } return loadFromDatabase() // waited a second: load it ourselves } } private fun run(label: String, pods: Int, strategy: (Pod) -> String) { val fleet = List(pods) { Pod() } fleet[0].redis.del(KEY, "lock:$KEY") dbCalls.set(0) val threads = Executors.newFixedThreadPool(100) val start = CountDownLatch(1) val requests = (0 until 100).map { i -> CompletableFuture.supplyAsync({ start.await(); strategy(fleet[i % pods]) }, threads) } val t0 = System.nanoTime() start.countDown() requests.forEach { it.join() } println("%-40s database calls: %3d %4d ms".format(label, dbCalls.get(), (System.nanoTime() - t0) / 1_000_000)) threads.shutdown() fleet.forEach { it.redis.close() } } fun main() { run("no protection, 1 pod", 1, Pod::plain) run("single-flight, 1 pod", 1, Pod::singleFlight) run("single-flight, 4 pods", 4, Pod::singleFlight) run("Redis lock (SET NX PX), 4 pods", 4, Pod::redisLock) }

try.expect: no protection, 1 pod prints database calls: 100, single-flight, 1 pod prints 1, single-flight, 4 pods prints 4, and Redis lock (SET NX PX), 4 pods prints 1. Every line takes about 205 to 245 ms, one query's time, because all 100 requests wait side by side. The lock costs a little more, because the losers check every 10 ms. The demo's fake database never slows down under load; a real one with 100 identical queries and a pool of 20 would make the first line much slower. If the lock holder crashes, the lock expires after 2,000 ms, and the waiters give up after about a second and load the row themselves. delex with CompareCondition.valueEq, which deletes the lock only if it still holds your token, needs Redis 8.4 or newer.

sections.h: Refresh early, at random: probabilistic early expiration
sections.html:
Single-flight and the lock make a stampede smaller. Refreshing a busy key before it expires avoids the miss altogether, if you can decide who refreshes, and when. A timer for every key is a lot of machinery for a cache. A fixed window, such as "reload when less than 10 seconds are left", has a stampede of its own: every read inside the window starts a reload.

Let's size the problem first. A 2015 paper by Vattani, Chierichetti and Lowenstein, which calls its method XFetch, puts it as arithmetic. Take a key that is read 10 times a second and takes 3 seconds to recompute. When it expires, it gets about 30 recomputations: one for every read that arrives before the first recompute finishes.

XFetch lets each reader decide alone, at random. Next to the value, store how long its last recompute took (delta) and when it expires. On every read, recompute early if this is true:

now - delta * beta * ln(rand()) >= expiry

rand() is a random number between 0 and 1, and ln is the natural logarithm, a button on a scientific calculator. For a number between 0 and 1, ln gives a negative result, so -ln(rand()) is a positive random number: usually around 1, sometimes 3 or 4, very rarely more. The reader pretends it's a little later than it is, by delta times that number, and recomputes if the pretend time is past the expiry. Far from the deadline, almost nobody does. Within a few recompute times of it, the odds climb fast, so usually one reader refreshes a little early while everyone else keeps reading the old value. beta, 1 by default, scales how early: above 1, refreshes start earlier and stampedes get rarer.

Why this odd formula, and not a random moment in a fixed window? The paper proves that a fixed window must open far too early. Take an item rebuilt once a day, with a one-minute rebuild and 10,000 reads a minute. To cut the stampede to 100 recomputations, a fixed window has to open about 50 minutes before the deadline. XFetch with beta = 1 starts about ln 10,000 ≈ 9.2 rebuild times early, about 9 minutes, and its expected stampede is about 2.4 recomputations. The paper also proves that no rule that doesn't know how often the key is read can do better.

In Redis, keep delta in a hash next to the value. Read the time left with PTTL in the same pipeline, a batch of commands sent together without waiting for each answer. Or store the expiry in the hash too, as the paper suggests for caches that can't report one. The demo plays the paper's example on a pretend clock.

That's the limit of everything in this lesson. These tools make a miss cheaper or rarer, but none of them makes a cached copy correct. The race from the simulator can still leave an old row in the cache until its TTL ends.

try.title: Count the recomputations, with and without XFetch
steps: Run XFetchDemo (Java) or XFetchDemoKt (Kotlin) from the labs folder. It needs no Redis. It simulates 10 hours of one busy key on a pretend clock, with reads arriving at random about 10 times a second, a 3-second recompute and a 60-second TTL.
Predict the plain TTL's "per refresh" number from the paper's arithmetic before you look. Then predict whether XFetch does more or fewer recomputations per hour in total.
Change beta on the last line to 0.5 and run it again. What happens to the stampede size, and to how early refreshes start?

code.title: XFetchDemo.java
code.html: package sfz.cache.l06.demo; import java.util.ArrayList; import java.util.List; import java.util.Random; /** * A hot key on a simulated clock: about 10 reads a second, a recompute that takes 3 seconds, a TTL of 60. * How many recomputations does each refresh cost with a plain TTL, and with XFetch? */ public class XFetchDemo { static final double TTL = 60, DELTA = 3, RATE = 10, HOURS = 10; static void simulate(String label, double beta) { Random random = new Random(42); // same seed, same reads, in Java and Kotlin double expiry = TTL; // the value was computed at t = 0 List<Double> finishing = new ArrayList<>(); // recomputes in flight: when each one ends List<Integer> perRefresh = new ArrayList<>(); // recomputes started for each refresh int started = 0, misses = 0, recomputes = 0; double earlySum = 0; for (double t = 0; t < HOURS * 3600; t += -Math.log(1 - random.nextDouble()) / RATE) { for (int i = finishing.size() - 1; i >= 0; i--) { // a finished recompute stores a fresh value if (finishing.get(i) <= t) { double newExpiry = finishing.remove(i) + TTL; if (newExpiry > expiry) { expiry = newExpiry; if (started > 0) perRefresh.add(started); started = 0; } } } boolean recompute; if (t >= expiry) { // nothing fresh to return: a miss misses++; recompute = true; } else if (beta > 0) { // XFetch: now - delta * beta * ln(rand) >= expiry double u = 1 - random.nextDouble(); // uniform in (0, 1] recompute = t - DELTA * beta * Math.log(u) >= expiry; if (recompute) earlySum += expiry - t; } else { recompute = false; } if (recompute) { started++; recomputes++; finishing.add(t + DELTA); } } double mean = perRefresh.stream().mapToInt(Integer::intValue).average().orElse(0); int max = perRefresh.stream().mapToInt(Integer::intValue).max().orElse(0); int early = recomputes - misses; System.out.printf("%-17s per refresh: %4.1f recomputes (max %2d) reads that missed: %5d recomputes per hour: %4.0f%s%n", label, mean, max, misses, recomputes / HOURS, early > 0 ? String.format(" started %.1f s early on average", earlySum / early) : ""); } public static void main(String[] args) { System.out.printf("A hot key, %.0f hours: ~%.0f reads/s, %.0f s to recompute, TTL %.0f s%n", HOURS, RATE, DELTA, TTL); simulate("plain TTL", 0); simulate("XFetch, beta 1", 1); simulate("XFetch, beta 2", 2); } }

alt.title: XFetchDemo.kt
alt.html: package sfz.cache.l06.demo import java.util.Random import kotlin.math.ln /** * A hot key on a simulated clock: about 10 reads a second, a recompute that takes 3 seconds, a TTL of 60. * How many recomputations does each refresh cost with a plain TTL, and with XFetch? */ private const val TTL = 60.0 private const val DELTA = 3.0 private const val RATE = 10.0 private const val HOURS = 10.0 private fun simulate(label: String, beta: Double) { val random = Random(42) // same seed, same reads, in Java and Kotlin var expiry = TTL // the value was computed at t = 0 val finishing = mutableListOf<Double>() // recomputes in flight: when each one ends val perRefresh = mutableListOf<Int>() // recomputes started for each refresh var started = 0 var misses = 0 var recomputes = 0 var earlySum = 0.0 var t = 0.0 while (t < HOURS * 3600) { for (i in finishing.indices.reversed()) { // a finished recompute stores a fresh value if (finishing[i] <= t) { val newExpiry = finishing.removeAt(i) + TTL if (newExpiry > expiry) { expiry = newExpiry if (started > 0) perRefresh += started started = 0 } } } val recompute = when { t >= expiry -> { misses++; true } // nothing fresh to return: a miss beta > 0 -> { // XFetch: now - delta * beta * ln(rand) >= expiry val u = 1 - random.nextDouble() // uniform in (0, 1] (t - DELTA * beta * ln(u) >= expiry).also { if (it) earlySum += expiry - t } } else -> false } if (recompute) { started++ recomputes++ finishing += t + DELTA } t += -ln(1 - random.nextDouble()) / RATE } val early = recomputes - misses println("%-17s per refresh: %4.1f recomputes (max %2d) reads that missed: %5d recomputes per hour: %4.0f%s".format( label, perRefresh.average(), perRefresh.max(), misses, recomputes / HOURS, if (early > 0) " started %.1f s early on average".format(earlySum / early) else "")) } fun main() { println("A hot key, %.0f hours: ~%.0f reads/s, %.0f s to recompute, TTL %.0f s".format(HOURS, RATE, DELTA, TTL)) simulate("plain TTL", 0.0) simulate("XFetch, beta 1", 1.0) simulate("XFetch, beta 2", 2.0) }

try.expect: plain TTL per refresh: 30.8 recomputes (max 48) reads that missed: 16790 recomputes per hour: 1679: the paper's 10 × 3 = 30, and every one of them is a read that found nothing to return. XFetch, beta 1 per refresh: 2.7 recomputes (max 16) reads that missed: 0 recomputes per hour: 188 started 9.0 s early on average, close to the paper's expected 2.4. XFetch, beta 2 prints 1.6 per refresh (max 8), 164 an hour, and 25.3 s early. So XFetch refreshes a little more often than once per TTL, and still does about a ninth of the plain TTL's work, because each refresh costs one or two recomputations instead of thirty. Java and Kotlin print the same numbers, because both use java.util.Random with seed 42, a fixed starting point for the random numbers. With beta 0.5, the last line becomes 6.8 recomputes per refresh (max 34), 288 reads that missed, and 2.4 s early: refreshing later brings part of the stampede back.

opening:
Picture a bakery with a shelf of bread by the door. Customers take a loaf and go. When the shelf is empty, a customer asks the baker at the back, who takes a while to bake one. At nine, the shelf empties with a hundred customers in the shop, and all of them ask the baker for the same loaf. The baker bakes the same bread a hundred times while every other order waits.

The payments app has a shelf like that: Redis, a program that keeps data in memory, holding copies of records from its slower database. It's easy to believe a cache can only take load off the database, since every copy found in it is a query saved. On average, that's true. At the moment a busy copy expires, the cache sends everyone to the database at once.

In Expiry, eviction and memory, we gave every key a deadline. In this lesson, we'll use Redis as a cache, compare five ways to run one, and stop a stampede three ways. Before we start, make a guess, and keep it in mind.
closing:
We started with a bakery shelf that emptied at nine, and a hundred customers asking the baker for the same loaf. Cache-aside fills the shelf, and jitter staggers the sell-by dates. Single-flight and a lock send one customer to the back, and XFetch bakes the next loaf before the shelf runs out.

If Redis is still running from the Try its, run INFO stats and compare keyspace_hits with keyspace_misses. Those two numbers are your hit ratio.

Next, we'll take apart the race that commit-then-delete still allows, and find out how an old row gets back into the cache after it was deleted.

compare.title: Cache-aside with a negative marker, in Java and Kotlin

java.title: MerchantCache.java
java.html: public Merchant get(String id) { String cached = redis.get("merchant:" + id); if (cached != null) { // a hit: a row or the marker return MISSING.equals(cached) ? null : Merchant.decode(cached); } Merchant m = repository.find(id); // a miss: the slow part if (m == null) { redis.set("merchant:" + id, MISSING, SetParams.setParams().ex(60)); } else { redis.set("merchant:" + id, m.encode(), SetParams.setParams().ex(jitteredTtl(3_600, 0.1, random))); } return m; }

kotlin.title: MerchantCache.kt
kotlin.html: fun get(id: String): Merchant? { redis.get("merchant:$id")?.let { cached -> // a hit: a row or the marker return if (cached == MISSING) null else Merchant.decode(cached) } val m: Merchant? = repository.find(id) // a miss: the slow part if (m == null) { redis.set("merchant:$id", MISSING, SetParams.setParams().ex(60)) } else { redis.set("merchant:$id", m.encode(), SetParams.setParams().ex(jitteredTtl(3_600, 0.1, random))) } return m }

compare.note: Both send the same traffic to Redis: one GET, and on a miss one SET with a TTL that depends on what the database said. Both use Jedis, the Java library this track uses to talk to Redis. Kotlin's ?.let { return ... } turns the hit into an early return, and its types make the three outcomes visible: redis.get returns String?, a string that may be null (not cached), MISSING maps to a null Merchant? (known missing), and anything else decodes into a row. Java gets the same result with explicit null checks. Neither version handles the stampede yet; the lab adds single-flight in front of the database call.

worked.title: Stop a stampede across copies of the app with a Redis lock

steps.say: Start from the hit: only a miss needs any coordination. On a miss, try to become the one copy that loads. SET lock:<key> <token> NX PX 2000 succeeds for exactly one caller, because Redis runs each command to the end, one at a time, on its single thread (Inside an in-memory store: how Redis executes commands). The token is a random value that says whose lock it is.
steps.code: String v = redis.get(key); if (v != null) return v; String token = UUID.randomUUID().toString(); boolean leader = redis.set("lock:" + key, token, SetParams.setParams().nx().px(2_000)) != null;

alt.html: redis.get(key)?.let { return it } val token = UUID.randomUUID().toString() val leader = redis.set("lock:$key", token, SetParams.setParams().nx().px(2_000)) != null

steps.say: The leader loads the row, fills the cache, then releases the lock. Release only your own lock: if the load took longer than 2 seconds, the lock has expired and may belong to another copy by now. Redis 8.4's DELEX ... IFEQ deletes the key only if its value still matches. Before 8.4, it takes a three-line Lua script that compares and deletes, like the scripts in Keeping a cache honest: invalidation, leases and consistency.
steps.code: if (leader) { try { String row = loadFromDatabase(key); redis.set(key, row, SetParams.setParams().ex(jitteredTtl(3_600, 0.1, random))); return row; } finally { redis.delex("lock:" + key, CompareCondition.valueEq(token)); } }

alt.html: if (leader) { try { return loadFromDatabase(key).also { redis.set(key, it, SetParams.setParams().ex(jitteredTtl(3_600, 0.1, random))) } } finally { redis.delex("lock:$key", CompareCondition.valueEq(token)) } }

steps.say: Everyone else waits for the cache, briefly. Check every 10 ms for up to a second. If the leader died, stop waiting and load it yourself: a second load is wasted work, not a wrong answer.
steps.code: for (int i = 0; i < 100; i++) { Thread.sleep(10); String row = redis.get(key); if (row != null) return row; } return loadFromDatabase(key); // the leader is gone or slow: load anyway

alt.html: repeat(100) { Thread.sleep(10) redis.get(key)?.let { return it } } return loadFromDatabase(key) // the leader is gone or slow: load anyway

steps.say: Measure it. In the lesson's demo, 4 pods with 25 requests each, all at once, made 4 database calls with single-flight in each pod and 1 with the lock, at about the same speed. In a real app, use both: single-flight first, so only one thread in each copy even tries for the lock.

lab.title: Single-flight, then a cache-aside cache with jitter and negative entries
steps: Start Docker, then run the tests from the labs folder with the command above. Gradle is the tool that builds the labs' Java and Kotlin code and runs their tests. All 15 fail at first: six in SingleFlightTest and two in JitteredTtlTest need no Docker, and seven in MerchantCacheTest use a real Redis in a container that all the tests share. The database in the tests is a fake that sleeps and counts its calls.

In SingleFlight.kt, write load. Its comment gives the three steps: claim the key with putIfAbsent, follow by joining the leader's future, or lead by loading and completing your own future. Run ./gradlew :redis:test --tests 'sfz.cache.l06.SingleFlightTest' until its six tests pass.

Write get: GET the key, decode a hit (the marker means null), and on a miss go through flights.load(id, () -> ...). Inside the loader, GET once more, then ask the repository (the class that reads shops from the database) and SET with the right TTL.
Run all 15 tests. Read a hundred concurrent misses for one merchant reach the repository once: it's frame 5 of the stepper, with a real Redis.
hints: flights.putIfAbsent(key, mine) returns null when you claimed the key. Kotlin's ?: gives a short shape: val running = flights.putIfAbsent(key, mine) ?: return lead(...).
join() wraps the leader's exception in a CompletionException. Catch it and throw e.cause ?: e, so followers see the same IllegalStateException as the leader.
Remove the entry in a finally block with flights.remove(key, mine), the two-argument form: it removes the entry only if it's still your own future.
In Java, flights.load(id, () -> { ... return m; }) works because a Kotlin () -> V is a Function0<V>, which a Java lambda can implement.

drill.title: Single-flight from memory
drill.prompt: Close the lab. Write load(key, loader) for single-flight, using a ConcurrentHashMap<String, CompletableFuture<V>>. Allow one loader call per key at a time. Followers get the leader's value or its exception, and the entry disappears when the load ends. Then compare with the answer. Which line makes sure only one caller leads?

answer.html: V load(String key, Supplier<V> loader) { CompletableFuture<V> mine = new CompletableFuture<>(); CompletableFuture<V> running = flights.putIfAbsent(key, mine); // atomic: exactly one caller gets null if (running != null) { try { return running.join(); } catch (CompletionException e) { throw e.getCause() instanceof RuntimeException r ? r : e; } } try { V value = loader.get(); mine.complete(value); return value; } catch (RuntimeException e) { mine.completeExceptionally(e); throw e; } finally { flights.remove(key, mine); // not a cache: the next miss loads again } }

alt.html: fun load(key: String, loader: () -> V): V { val mine = CompletableFuture<V>() val running = flights.putIfAbsent(key, mine) // atomic: exactly one caller gets null if (running != null) { try { return running.join() } catch (e: CompletionException) { throw e.cause ?: e } } try { return loader().also { mine.complete(it) } } catch (e: Throwable) { mine.completeExceptionally(e) throw e } finally { flights.remove(key, mine) // not a cache: the next miss loads again } }

recap: Cache-aside: GET from Redis; on a miss, load from the database and SET with a TTL. Redis never talks to the database, and the TTL is how long a wrong answer may live.

The five patterns differ in who loads and who writes. Read-through and write-through hand that to a library, write-behind leaves the cache holding the only copy until it writes the database, and refresh-ahead reloads before expiry.
On a write, commit to the database, then DEL the key. Give every entry a TTL, because it caps every race that's left.
Add jitter to TTLs (for example 3,600 s ± 10%) so keys loaded together don't expire together, and cache "not found" with a short TTL.

A busy key's expiry is a stampede. Single-flight collapses the misses inside one running program, and a SET NX PX lock in Redis does it across copies of the app. XFetch refreshes early at random, so one or two readers refresh a little before the deadline instead of thirty after it.
The limit: these tools make misses cheaper or rarer, but none makes a cached copy correct. A slow reader can still put an old row back after the delete.

explain.prompt: The person who runs the database asks why its query rate for the merchants table jumps to 40 times normal at ten past every hour, for about a minute. The app caches shops in Redis with EX 3600, and a job fills the cache whenever a new version of the app starts. Explain what's happening and what you'll change.
explain.answer: The job loaded every shop within about a minute, all with exactly 3,600 seconds of TTL, so they all expire within the same minute an hour later. During that minute, every read of every shop misses and goes to the database, the rows are reloaded with exactly 3,600 seconds again, and the spike repeats every hour. Busy shops make it worse: when one expires, every request for it that arrives before the first reload finishes also misses, so the same row is queried dozens of times at once. I'll add jitter, for example 3,600 seconds plus or minus 10%, so the expiries spread over 12 minutes and stay spread. And I'll put single-flight in front of the database call, so each copy of the app loads a given shop once, with a short Redis lock for the few busiest shops, so only one copy loads them.

deeper.html:
Client-side caching moves the cache into your own program and lets Redis tell you when to drop an entry. It needs RESP3, the newest version of the message format that Redis and its clients use. A connection can turn on tracking: Redis remembers which keys that client read, and sends a message on the same connection when one of them changes, expires or is evicted. Jedis 8 builds this in with .cacheConfig(CacheConfig.builder().maxSize(1000).build()) on a RESP3 client. A hit then costs no network trip at all. The price is server memory for the tracking table (or broadcasting by prefix instead, where clients ask for messages about every key that starts with a given prefix), and a short window after a write in which other clients' local copies are still old.

Serving stale data is the simplest stampede fix of all, for data that can take it. Keep a second, longer-lived copy (or a soft deadline inside the value), answer with the old row while one loader refreshes it, and never let readers wait. Meta, the company behind Facebook, does a version of this in its memcache system: right after a delete, a reader may get the deleted value marked as stale instead of waiting, and most of its applications can use that as it is. Keeping a cache honest: invalidation, leases and consistency shows the lease that goes with it.

XFetch trades total work for smaller stampedes. Each refresh starts a little early, so a key is recomputed a little more often than its TTL alone would ask. But each refresh costs one or two recomputations instead of thirty, and no reader ever finds the key missing. The paper's experiments replayed a week of requests for one popular item and found that the exponential rule held up under bursts, where fixed windows of early expiry did not.
